title: Activation Mirroring and Cross-Plane Commit Protocol (WIP)
content:
Summary:

This note sketches an approach for reducing cold- and warm-start token latency on multi-GPU inference by combining a lightweight activation mirroring mechanism with a cross-plane commit protocol for KV cache updates. The intent is to enable low-latency local KV hits for common prefixes without sacrificing eventual consistency and to provide deterministic fallback semantics when mirrors are stale or partially available.

Motivation / Problem Statement:

- In production workloads we see a distribution of requests where a small number of recent prefixes generate a disproportionate share of tokens. When those prefixes map to KV shards on remote GPUs, we pay a large latency tax for cross-GPU lookups (PCIe/NVLink + NCCL).
- Existing approaches rely on single-shot prefetching or coarse-grained replication which either over-replicate memory or introduce expensive synchronous transfers at request time.
- We need an approach that: (1) maximizes local cache hit rate for hot prefixes, (2) keeps memory overhead bounded, and (3) provides clear correctness/fallback semantics for model cache coherence under rollouts and retries.

Goals / Success Criteria:

- p95 token generation latency reduction for cold/warm prefixes by >= 20% for 90% of traffic.
- Keep additional GPU memory overhead < 10% for mirrored activations on typical LLMs (7B–70B ranges).
- KV cache staleness window < 1s for non-evicted keys under normal steady-state.
- Detect and safely fallback on mismatch cases without introducing >5% error rate for generation quality (deterministic unit tests).

High-level idea:

1) Activation mirroring: we maintain a small, approximate mirror of recently written KV entries (keys + compressed/quantized activations) on GPUs that are likely to serve requests for those prefixes. Mirrors are intentionally size-limited and approximate (FP16/8 or quantized blocks) to save memory. Mirroring is asynchronous and best-effort.

2) Cross-plane commit protocol: when a write/update to the canonical KV shard occurs (e.g., after producing activations for a new token), the owning plane emits a compact commit record to a cross-plane commit stream. Mirrors subscribe to this stream and apply lightweight updates to their local mirrors. Each commit has an epoch id and monotonic sequence number; mirrors track the highest committed epoch they have applied.

3) Local-first lookup with verification: on a request, the runtime attempts a local mirror lookup first. If a local hit is found, the runtime uses the mirrored activation but simultaneously issues an async verification to the canonical shard (a compact hash check). If verification fails or times out, the runtime triggers a transparent local fallback: fetch the canonical activation (blocking) and mark the mirrored entry as stale.

Design details:

Activation mirror layout:
- Mirror entries store: key-hash (64-bit), compressed activation blob, commit_seq (u64), insertion_ts (ms), refcount (for active sessions).
- Compression: use 8-bit quantized blocks for layer-normed activations with a small lookup table for scaling; optionally use FP16 for larger-memory GPUs.
- Per-GPU mirror memory budget is configurable per deployment profile; default target = 6% of model activation RAM.

Cross-plane commit stream:
- Commit records are tiny: {key-hash, commit_seq, source-plane-id, short-hash-of-blob}. The canonical plane also exposes a short HTTP/gRPC verify endpoint (key-hash -> commit_seq + short-hash) for rapid verification.
- Commit propagation uses NCCL-backed async allgather for high-throughput setups or a light TCP-based publish-subscribe layer for multi-host/private deployments without shared NVLink.

Local-first lookup + verification flow (pseudocode):
- lookup(key):
  - if mirror.contains(key) -> use mirror.activation; spawn async verify(key, mirror.commit_seq)
  - else -> perform remote fetch from canonical shard (blocking), then optionally insert into mirror asynchronously
- verify(key, seq):
  - call verify endpoint on canonical plane; if canonical_seq > seq or short-hash mismatch -> invalidate mirror entry; if missing -> block-fetch on next request

Consistency and invariants:
- Strong invariant: canonical shard is the source-of-truth; mirrors are read-only caches with monotonic commit_seq.
- Mirrors do not accept writes from local inference code; all writes go to canonical plane which issues commits. This avoids split-brain for updates during rollouts.

NCCL / transport considerations:

- For intra-host NVLink/NVSwitch topologies, use a light NCCL async broadcast or segmented ring: commits are tiny and can be batched into multi-key frames to amortize launch/latency. Assess trade-offs between many small launches vs batched launches with slightly higher latency.
- For inter-host clusters (no NVLink), use a small raft-ish leader for commit propagation or a dedicated UDP/TCP pub-sub mesh (gossip) with bounded staleness guarantees.
- Tune NCCL: set aggressiveness of transport aggregation by traffic class (commit stream = latency-sensitive tiny messages -> prefer small batch sizes and prioritized lanes; large KV transfers = throughput-focused). Use NCCL stream priorities where supported to avoid head-of-line blocking.

Eviction and memory management:
- Mirror eviction is LRU with session-aware pinning; recently used prefixes and in-flight sessions pin entries to avoid repeated misses when serving multi-token responses.
- On eviction, mirrors emit a compact tombstone to commit stream to ensure other mirrors don't rely on stale short-hash matches. Tombstones carry the last_commit_seq.

Performance experiments (planned):
- Microbench harness that simulates the observed prefix distribution: Zipf k=0.9 with 1M distinct prefixes; measure p50/p90/p95 latency with and without mirroring across 1/2/4/8 GPU layouts.
- PCIe/NVLink counters: track bytes/sec and saturation; measure mirror update rate vs canonical fetchs.
- Cache hit telemetry: target > 60% local hit rate for hot-1000 prefixes; measure false-positive verification rate.
- Fault injection: simulate missing commit records, stale mirrors, and rolling restarts to ensure deterministic fallback and no silent correctness regressions.

Implementation plan / milestones:
- Phase 0 (spike): implement lightweight commit stream prototype using existing NCCL transport; run single-host 4xA40 tests. (Owner: Marco)
- Phase 1 (prototype): add mirror structures + local-first lookup path inside runtime; enable verification API. Add metrics for hit/miss/verify-time. (Owner: Evelyn)
- Phase 2 (scale): integrate TCP-based commit mesh for multi-host; quantization pipeline stable; eviction policies tuned. (Owner: Asha)
- Phase 3 (rollout): gated rollout behind feature flag; A/B test on low-traffic customer routes; measure production SLOs before wider rollout.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Mirror fidelity vs memory: what's the sweet spot of quantization that avoids generator-quality regressions? Need quality evals on unit prompts.
- Commit propagation consistency: do we require total order for commits across planes? For correctness probably not — per-key monotonic seq is enough — but this complicates garbage collection and tombstone semantics.
- Cost of verification calls: synchronous verification adds a network hop; we want to keep verification async and rely on fast canonical verification endpoints, but must quantify the incident rate of verification failures and their cost.
- Security: commit stream must be authenticated and integrity-protected to prevent cross-tenant pollution in shared clusters.

TODOs:
- [Evelyn] build microbench harness and run zipf experiments for 1/4/8 GPU configs by 2024-12-09
- [Marco] prototype NCCL commit batching and measure launch overhead by 2024-12-16
- [Asha] run quantization/quality sweep on 7B and 33B checkpoints (automated evals) by 2024-12-20

Notes for reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic and best-effort: mirrors are caches, not replicas. The protocol is designed to keep the normal-path fast and make the fallback path correct and transparent. Please critique the verification fallback latency/overhead tradeoffs and whether per-key monotonic seqs are sufficient for our rollout semantics.

Appendix: lightweight verification API (sketch)
- GET /kv/verify?key_hash=<h>&seq=<s> -> {status: ok|stale|missing, canonical_seq: u64, short_hash: u32}
- Expected 95th pct response time < 0.6ms intra-host; < 2ms inter-host (optimized stack).

End of note.
